23.0.s.en: (1) David rules in the fear of God

23.0.0.en: David spoke the following words at the end of his life, stating that his words were a revelation to him from the Lord. He had been a simple shepherd of sheep, and God raised him up and entrusted him with the highest office by anointing him king to lead His people. He himself was the arranger of the sweet psalms with which he sang to the Lord.

23.0.1.en: Singing is the work of the angels, for they praise God day and night. Therefore one of the most beautiful things a person can do is to sing and praise the Lord, so that he is filled with peace and joy, his troubles vanish, and he enjoys the vision of God and fellowship with Him.

23.1.0.en: David did not speak from himself; rather his words were a revelation from the Holy Spirit, and the Lord spoke through his tongue.

23.2.0.en: David affirmed that the One who spoke is the God of Israel and their Rock on whom they rely, and he says that when the righteous king rules his people, he rules them with justice and in the fear of God.

23.3.0.en: After the rain: after the rainfall.

23.3.1.en: Such a king is a guide to his people and lights the way for them, as the light of the sun shines when it rises in the morning. He leads them to fulfill their good aspirations, and his rule over them is a flourishing and splendid rule, as the grass of the field flourishes after it is watered by the rain.

23.4.0.en: The beautiful qualities of rule that David described in the preceding verses will be the qualities that adorn the manner of his rule and the rule of his descendants after him. They rest on righteousness, because his covenant with God is an everlasting covenant that does not end with the end of his life, but his descendants are bound by it from generation to generation. It is a firm and preserved covenant, and it confirms the continuance of his delight and joy and the fulfillment of his salvation.

23.4.1.en: We must remember that God's covenants are conditioned on a person's conduct in the fear of the Lord. It is good that we hold fast to His covenants and recall them persistently in our prayers, but we must know that the fulfillment of these covenants depends on how firmly we ourselves hold to God's commandments. Only the righteous enjoy God's covenants, which fill their lives with salvation and joy.

23.5.0.en: Belial: a pagan god, and "sons of Belial" is a name given to the wicked who do not fear the Lord. As for the wicked from whom nothing good is to be expected, David likened them to thorns thrown on the ground, worthless. A person does not try to take hold of them with his hand, because the sharp points of the thorns will wound him; they harm everyone who deals with them. Therefore whoever wants to touch them must deal with them with severity and force, using strong tools such as iron and the staff of a spear, so that he is safe from injury and guards against the pricking of the thorns, and deals with them from a distance without hurting his hands. If he strikes them with the staff of a spear and with iron, these wicked ones perish in their place.

23.6.s.en: (2) The heroes of the first rank

23.6.0.en: David was concerned to put capabilities to work and to establish and organize leaders. Therefore this chapter lists the names of his mighty men who supported him in his wars. The list begins with the names of three heroes of the first rank, that is, those who surpassed the others in courage, valor and military rank. They are: Josheb-basshebeth the Tachmonite, or the Hachmonite, who is the same as Jashobeam as mentioned in (1 Chr 11:11). He used his spear in the wars against David's enemies and killed 800 soldiers of the enemy.

23.6.1.en: (In Chronicles (1 Chr 11:11) it is said that the number of those he killed was 300. The explanation of this difference is that Josheb himself killed 300 warriors with his own hands, while the men of his company killed the remaining five hundred, so the whole work was attributed to him figuratively. Josheb was regarded as the chief of the first three heroes.

23.7.1.en: The second hero is Eleazar the son of Dodo the son of an Ahohite, who joined David in fighting the Philistines at a place called "Dammim," west of Judah. When the Philistines went out to battle and the men of Israel withdrew, this hero remained alone defying the Philistines, and he kept fighting them until his hands were weary from striking them, and he killed a great number of them. Since his hand clung to the sword for a long time, it almost stuck to it, and he found it difficult to open his grip from the sword. When the men of Israel saw him achieving this great victory, they gathered again and went after him to plunder the belongings of the slain and the spoils of war.

23.8.0.en: The third hero is Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. His heroism came when the Philistines attacked the children of Israel in a field planted with lentils. The children of Israel were afraid and left the field when Shammah confronted the Philistines alone, for he stood in the midst of the field and delivered it from the hand of the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, and the Lord wrought a great salvation by his hand.

23.9.0.en: The cave of Adullam: it lies west of Bethlehem.

23.9.1.en: After speaking of the individual feats of heroism achieved by each of the first three heroes, the inspired text mentions here a collective heroic deed done by the three together. This heroic deed took place during the first war with the Philistines, after David had taken Jerusalem (ch. 5:17-21). The war was in the hot days of summer, at harvest time, and David was then in the cave of Adullam to make his war plans, while the Philistines were gathered in "the valley of Rephaim."

23.10.0.en: The garrison of the Philistines: detachments from the army of the Philistines.

23.10.1.en: David was staying in the stronghold, which is the cave, while some detachments of the Philistine army had taken Bethlehem and prepared to fight David.

23.11.0.en: In this extremely hot weather David became very thirsty, and he expressed his thirst by longing for the well of Bethlehem, which is at the gate of the city where he was born and raised.

23.12.0.en: It grieved the first three heroes to see their king sighing from the intensity of his thirst, so they risked their lives and broke through the camp of the Philistines with all boldness and courage until they reached the well, and they drew water and returned with it to David to quench his thirst. But David saw that this water was very costly, for its price was the blood of his heroes, because they had exposed themselves to death in order to bring it. So he refused to drink it and poured it out on the ground before God, and he said that he refused to quench his thirst with a drink of water that had been brought by his heroic men putting their lives in danger.

23.12.1.en: May you be austere and detached, not seeking your own comfort at the expense of others, and inclined to self-giving rather than selfishness, just as David refused to give himself comfort at the expense of his enemies, and his heart pricked him because he had asked for water from a well held by the enemies. And be, on the contrary, ready to toil for the sake of others in order to give them rest.

23.13.s.en: (3) The heroes of the second rank

23.13.0.en: The following verses recount the feats of heroism done by the three heroes of the second rank, beginning with the first of them and their chief, Abishai the brother of Joab, who killed three hundred of the enemy's soldiers by himself and so deserved to have a position of leadership among the three heroes.

23.14.0.en: Abishai was the most capable of the heroes of the second rank, so he was regarded as their chief, but in his feats of heroism he did not reach the standing of the first three, "Josheb, Eleazar and Shammah."

23.15.0.en: Kabzeel: in the south of Judah, and it is now Khirbet Hura.

23.15.1.en: The second hero in this group is "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada," who was chief over the Cherethites and the Pelethites under David (ch. 20:23). He was the son of the high priest in the days of David and became the commander of Solomon's army (1 Kgs 4:4). The inspired text says of him that he was a strong man who had done many great deeds, and that he was originally from the town of Kabzeel. The inspired text relates some of his heroic deeds: in one of them he killed two lions that were coming out of the land of Moab and devouring people, and he confronted them and killed them. The second heroic deed was his entering the den of a lion, on a day when the lion was sheltering in it from the rain and the cold, and he killed the lion. The third heroic deed was his killing a mighty Egyptian man who used to attack people and trouble and harm them. He killed him in a manner similar to the story of David and Goliath the Philistine, for he went down to him with no weapon but a staff, and struck him and took his spear from him and killed him with it.

23.16.0.en: His confidants: those close to the king, who know his secrets and keep them, such as military secrets.

23.16.1.en: These heroic deeds of Benaiah made his name among the three of the second rank, so that he held a higher position than the three who are of the third rank, but in standing he did not reach the first three. The inspired text did not mention the name of the third hero in this group, and perhaps he is Amasa, to whom David promised that he would become the commander of his army.

23.16.2.en: If you rely on God, He will give you mighty strength, and you will overcome your enemies the demons, however great their power, and you will even lead others in the way of the spiritual life, so that you stand firm in God and serve Him and enjoy His work in you.

23.17.0.en: From here the inspired text mentions thirty other heroes who form the third class of heroes. They are:

23.17.1.en: Asahel: the brother of Joab and Abishai, whom Abner killed in self-defense (ch. 2:23). Elhanan the son of Dodo: his homeland was Bethlehem.

23.18.0.en: Shammah the Harodite: from the town of "Harod," whose site is now "Khirbet Hazidan," lying about 5 km southeast of Jerusalem. He is also called "Shammoth the Harorite" in (1 Chr 11:27), and he is the same as "Shamhuth the Izrahite" in (1 Chr 27:8). Elika the Harodite: he is also from Harod.

23.19.0.en: Helez the Paltite: he is the same as "the Pelonite" (1 Chr 11:27), and he is from the tribe of Ephraim.

23.19.1.en: Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: from the town of Tekoa, from which came the wise woman of Tekoa (ch. 14), and Tekoa lies about 5 km southeast of Bethlehem.

23.20.0.en: Abiezer the Anethothite: from "Anathoth," the town of the prophet Jeremiah, which is today a small village named "Anata," 4 km from Jerusalem.

23.20.1.en: Mebunnai the Hushathite: he is the same as "Sibbechai" in (1 Chr 11:29, 2 Sam 21:18), and his homeland was "Hushah," which is now the village of "Husan," southwest of Bethlehem.

23.21.0.en: Zalmon the Ahohite: he is the same as "Ilai" in (1 Chr 11:29), and he was called the Ahohite after one of his ancestors.

23.21.1.en: Maharai the Netophathite: from the tribe of Judah, of the descendants of Zerah (1 Chr 27:13), and he is from Netophah, whose site is now Khirbet "Yad Faluh," which is 8 km south of Bethlehem.

23.22.0.en: Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite: he has another name, "Heled" (1 Chr 11:30), and he is also from Netophah.

23.22.1.en: Ittai the son of Ribai: from Gibeah, the birthplace of Saul.

23.23.0.en: Benaiah the Pirathonite: from Pirathon, one of the cities of Ephraim. It is now "Fara'ata," about 12 km southwest of Nablus.

23.23.1.en: Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash: these are among the valleys near the heights of Mount Gaash in the land of Ephraim, and it lies northeast of Lod by about 20 km.

23.24.0.en: Abialbon the Arbathite: named for "Beth-arabah," which is now "Ain al-Arabah" in the valley of al-Qilt.

23.24.1.en: Azmaveth the Barhumite: or "the Baharumite" (1 Chr 11:33), named for "Bahurim," which is now "Ras al-Tamim," near the Mount of Olives.

23.25.0.en: Eliahba the Shaalbonite: from "Shaalbin" or "Shaalabbin," which is now Salbit, lying about 3 km north of Ajlun.

23.25.1.en: Jonathan of the sons of Jashen: "Jashen" is also called "Hashem" (1 Chr 11:34).

23.26.0.en: Shammah the Hararite: he is the same as Shammah, one of the first chiefs (v. 11), and he is mentioned here because he was one of those serving under the command of Asahel, but he excelled in war and so was counted among the first three. Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite: Arar is the same as "Harar" (v. 11).

23.27.0.en: Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite: he is also called "Abiphelet" and "Eliphal" (1 Chr 11:35). He is attributed to one of his ancestors, "the Maachathite," that is, his origin is from "Maacah," a small kingdom in the northeast of Palestine (2 Sam 10:6). Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite: the son of Ahithophel, David's counselor, who followed Absalom, and he is from "Giloh," which was described earlier.

23.28.0.en: Hezrai the Carmelite: his name is also "Hezro" (1 Chr 11:37), and he is a native of "Carmel," whose site is now a ruin of the same name, 11 km northeast of "Hebron." Paarai the Arbite: he is also called "Naarai" (1 Chr 11:37), and he is from a town named "Arab" in Judea, in its hill country.

23.29.0.en: Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah: he is from the kingdom of Aram-zobah, which lies west of the Euphrates. Bani the Gadite: from the tribe of Gad.

23.30.0.en: Zelek the Ammonite: of the children of Ammon.

23.30.1.en: Naharai the Beerothite: the armorbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, and he is from Beeroth, one of the cities of the Gibeonites in the portion of Benjamin, and its name now is "al-Bireh."

23.31.0.en: Ira the Ithrite: named for the founder of the family, "Jether." Gareb the Ithrite: also of the descendants of "Jether."

23.32.0.en: Uriah the Hittite: whom David exposed to death unjustly in order to be rid of the traces of his sin, and he married his wife after he was killed.

23.32.1.en: The total is 37, among them the three heroes of the first rank, the three heroes of the second rank, and 31 heroes of the third rank, and the commander of them all was Joab.

23.32.2.en: It should be noted that the thirty-one are in truth only thirty, as stated in (v. 24), because Shammah is repeated, as we mentioned in (v. 33). We find that Joab is not mentioned here because it was known that he was the commander of all David's armies, and perhaps the reason he is not mentioned is his wrong in killing two innocent men, Abner and Amasa, in addition to his rebuking David. We also see that other names of David's heroes are mentioned in (1 Chr 11) that are not mentioned here, and this shows that there were many heroes by whom David's army was distinguished, as a divine grace supporting him. The mention of the lists of heroes proclaims the following:

23.32.3.en: 1- Honor and glorification for the striving of these heroes, and God's appreciation of them, so that their names are remembered throughout the generations.

23.32.4.en: 2- Glorification and exaltation of David, who took care to train them, coordinate their work, and give them the opportunity for their heroic deeds to appear.

23.32.5.en: 3- A proclamation of the faith of these heroes, which made God work by His power in them so that their heroic deeds appeared.

23.32.6.en: The Lord remembers for His beloved, the living and the departed, their striving and their works. The inspired text mentions their names in appreciation of what they offered, so as to make of them a good example for the faithful. So if we seek a portion like the portion of the saints, we must walk as they walked.
